Kim showed up just as the festival gates opened, wearing a shirt with Ukrainian embroidery over jeans, carrying a tin of shortbread her grandmother had made. She eyed the dishes. "You want me to be a bean?"

"Two beans, maybe," Sofia said. "What do I mark you as?"

Kim's fingers picked at the embroidery on her cuff. "At my gran's house I'm the Canadian one. At school I'm... I don't know. Sometimes it feels like camouflage, like I blend into whatever room I'm in and belong to none of them." She said it lightly, but she didn't look up.

"Then pick all of them," Sofia said, and held out the jar.

Kim hesitated, then took three beans and dropped them one by one. "Ukrainian. Scottish. And Metis, on my dad's side." A couple behind her, overhearing, laughed and said they'd need six beans, and their toddler got two.

By mid-afternoon the dishes held far more beans than people who had passed the booth, and the pattern matched the graph exactly. Sofia was staring at her chart when Ms. Chan stopped to buy a coffee, following her gaze.

"They let people report more than one origin on the census," Ms. Chan said. "It's been that way since 1981. That's why the totals run higher than the population."

Sofia looked at Kim, then at the crowded dishes, and reached for a marker to fix the graph's title. "Every bean counts," she said. "Grab a dish, Kim. We're not done counting."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A single sentence can mix both: in 'The new park, which cost two million dollars, is a waste,' the cost can be checked but 'a waste' is an opinion.
story:
Vincent set the folded newspaper next to his plate before he even sat down, and his father raised an eyebrow at it but said nothing until the spaghetti had been served. "You've been carrying that thing around since Tuesday," his father finally said. "Somebody die?" "Somebody wrote a letter," Vincent said. "About the skate park."

He smoothed the page flat between the salt shaker and his glass. The letter was short, and he had read it so many times he could almost recite it, but he read it aloud anyway, slower this time. "The new park, which cost two million dollars, is a waste." His mother twirled her fork and waited, the way she did when she suspected there was more coming.

There was more coming, but Vincent wasn't sure yet what it was. That was the problem. The letter had landed like a small bomb at school on Wednesday. Randy had marched around the cafeteria saying the writer was totally right, the whole thing was a boondoggle, while Ivana had pulled out her phone and started hunting for the town budget like a detective. Vincent had mostly watched them argue, feeling something he couldn't name, and then last night, lying in bed, he had grabbed a pencil and done something odd. He had drawn a line straight down the middle of the sentence.

"The two million dollars part is checkable," Ivana had said in the cafeteria, before the flash of the lunch lights and the clang of trays, and Vincent had nodded without really hearing her. Now, at the table, he heard it. He picked up his pencil, still tucked in the newspaper's fold, and drew the line again where his parents could see it. "Half of this sentence, you could go look up," he said. "The money part. Either the park cost two million dollars or it didn't, and the town records would say." He tapped the second half. "But this part, 'is a waste.' How would you check that?"

His father chewed for a moment. "You couldn't," he said slowly. "Somebody could think it's a waste and somebody else could think it's the best thing the town ever built, and both of them would just be saying what they think." "An opinion," Vincent's mother said. "The cost is the fact, and 'a waste' is the opinion." Vincent felt the pencil-line idea click into place, like the truce he and his cousin had once declared over a disputed Lego bin, each side keeping its half.

He thought of Randy tomorrow, still hot about the letter, and how Randy might resent being told his favorite argument was half made of fog. But Ivana would get it instantly. She already half had, in the cafeteria, with the porous afternoon light streaming through the window while she scrolled. Maybe he could just draw the line on a photocopy and hand it to both of them.

"So it's one sentence," Vincent said, "but it's doing two different jobs at the same time." His mother refilled his plate without being asked. "Pass me that pencil again," his father said. "Show me exactly where the line goes."

activity: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
knowledge_domain: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
fact: Natural selection acts on individuals, but it is populations that evolve; a single finch cannot grow a bigger beak because it needs one.
story:
The folded paper landed on Lea's lab stool just as the bell finished ringing. Inside, in Esteban's blocky handwriting: bet you can't explain the finches without saying "evolved" more than twice. She crumpled it into her pocket and looked up at the board, where Mr. Esposito had taped photographs of four finches side by side, each with a different beak.

"Islands," he said, tapping the map. "Same ancestor, different islands, different food. Your job today is to explain the beaks." He set a dish of sunflower seeds, a cup of sugar water, a bowl of dried nectar powder, and a tray of small hard beans on each bench. "Tools are on the side counter. Tweezers, pliers, nutcrackers, pipettes. Choose."

Lea's team got the beans. Zayn grabbed the pliers. "This is easy," he said, cracking three beans in a row. Lea picked up the tweezers and failed, twice, the beans skittering across the bench and rolling onto the floor. Her cheeks went hot. The bell would ring in twenty minutes, and she still had nothing for the bet, nothing for the write-up.

Esteban leaned over from the next bench, watching her fail with the tweezers a fourth time. "So the finches just grew bigger beaks to survive," he said. "Like, they needed them, so they got them."

"Think about it," Lea said. "My fingers didn't get stronger from failing just now." She held up the tweezers. "A single finch can't grow a bigger beak because it needs one. That's not how it works."

"Then where did the big beaks come from?"

Lea looked down the row of benches. At the nectar station, a girl was drawing liquid up through a pipette, quick and efficient, while her partner with the pliers dripped and fumbled. At the seed bench, Zayn's pliers flew. Every bench had a tool that won and tools that lost. She pulled her stool closer to Esteban.

"Some finches are just born with bigger beaks than others," she said. "Like, some are small, some are big, all in the same flock. It's random. Then the island decides."

"Decides how?"

"Look at Zayn." On their own bench, the pliers were crushing beans while her tweezers sat useless. "The ones with the right beak get the food. They survive, they have chicks, and the chicks get their beaks." She wrote it in the margin of her lab sheet, arrows branching out from one flock into many. "So the individual bird doesn't change. Not one bird. It's the whole population, over generations, that changes. That's the part that evolves."

Esteban frowned at his own paper. "So on the bean island, the big-beaked birds were the only ones that had chicks."

"And on the flower island, the skinny-beaked ones that could reach the nectar." Lea underlined her last line twice. Mr. Esposito walked past, paused, read over her shoulder, and moved on without a word. At the nectar bench, the pipette girl was doing a vigorous, splashy victory dance.

Lea tore a strip off the bottom of her lab sheet. She wrote one word, folded it, and flicked it across the aisle onto Esteban's bench. He opened it and found his own bet returned to him, with a tally mark underneath: she had used the word exactly once.

"Rematch on Friday," he whispered.

"Bring better tweezers."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, is marked by lighting small oil lamps called diyas and is usually celebrated over five days.
story:
Autumn arrived at her grandmother's house just as the sun was leaning low, carrying a box of small clay lamps that clinked together like teacups. The whole family was already there, aunts in the kitchen, uncles dragging chairs onto the porch, her little cousin circling the sweet table like a shark. Grandmother met Autumn at the door and put the box in her hands. "Line them along the window ledge before dark," she said, "and leave room for tomorrow."

Autumn set out the lamps carefully, one by one, curl of wick resting in each little clay bowl, until the ledge looked like a row of waiting boats. Tomorrow puzzled her. Festivals, as far as she knew, happened once and then ended, like birthdays. She counted the lamps, then counted the clay lamps still stacked in the box, and found that the box held many more than the ledge could hold in a single night. She counted the small bottles of oil too. Twelve. The ledge took only eight lamps. If the lamps were all meant for tonight, why bring enough oil for days?

She went to find her grandmother, who was in the kitchen telling an aunt exactly how much cardamom went into the syrup. "We call them diyas," Grandmother said when Autumn held one up, "the little oil lamps." Then she added, without stopping her stirring, "Diwali isn't just tonight. It goes for five days, and we light them each evening." Autumn did the arithmetic in her head. Eight lamps a night, five nights, and enough oil left over for mistakes. That was what the box had been telling her all along. She felt the same satisfaction she got when a math tutor at school showed her a shortcut and the numbers suddenly agreed with each other.

Next door, Mr. Papadopoulos was sweeping his porch, and he paused to watch the lamps begin to glow in the blue twilight. Autumn saw him standing there and carried a spare diya over the low wall between the yards, holding it carefully so the flame wouldn't gutter. "For your porch," she said. "It's Diwali, five nights of lights." He took it with both hands and set it on his step, where it burned small and steady beside his door.

Inside, her little cousin had excavated the bottom of the sweet tin, hunting for the last coconut barfi, and was holding it aloft in triumph when Autumn came back in. Grandmother was already at the window with the match, moving down the row, and one by one the ledge filled with light. "Tomorrow," she said, "you arrange them in the shape of a lotus." Autumn looked at the empty shelf below the window, already planning how the petals would go.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: In 1668 Francesco Redi put meat in jars; maggots grew in open jars, but not in jars covered with gauze that kept flies off the meat.
story:
Rosalie spread three jars on the garage workbench, each with a chunk of overripe banana inside, and pulled the gauze toward her like it was treasure. The whole thing had started at lunch, when Eugenie had banged her tray down and declared that rotting fruit made fruit flies all by itself, no flies needed. "The banana just turns into them," she had insisted. Rosalie couldn't stop thinking about it on the walk home, because if that were true, fruit flies were appearing out of nothing, and something about that bugged her more than the actual flies.

"You're building a fruit fly fortress," Samir said, ducking under the half-open garage door with a roll of masking tape. He had texted her that he wanted to see the experiment, and he had brought a headlamp for no reason Rosalie could figure out. She set jar one open on the bench. Jar two got a gauze cover, tied tight with string so nothing could sneak in or out. Jar three got a solid lid, completely sealed. "If flies come from the banana itself," she said, "then all three jars should get maggots. The cover shouldn't matter."

"But if flies come from flies," Samir said, "then covering the meat thwarts them." He pointed at jar two. "They'd land on the gauze and not get through." Rosalie nodded, though she hadn't thought of the word thwart. She had been calling it "blocking." Samir reached up to grab the string from a high shelf, and the headlamp slid off the workbench and cracked him square on the shoulder. He rubbed it, laughing. "Almost a concussion. That would have been a significant injury, and I would have sued your garage."

Mr. González, who was fixing a lawnmower two driveways over, wandered over when he saw the jars. He leaned against the doorframe, wiping his hands on a rag, and listened while Rosalie explained. "You know," he said, "a fellow named Francesco Redi did this back in 1668, only he used meat. Maggots grew in the open jars, but not in the ones he covered with gauze that kept the flies off the meat." He tapped jar two with one finger. "Same design, though. You'll see." Then he went back to his lawnmower without another word, which Rosalie appreciated.

For three days she checked the jars every afternoon, drawing what she saw in a notebook. The open jar grew wiggling white maggots on the banana. The gauze jar grew none, though on the second day Rosalie spotted two flies pacing across the mesh like tiny frustrated guards. The sealed jar grew nothing either, but it also smelled so terrible that Samir gagged and almost knocked it over holding his nose. On Thursday Eugenie showed up, arms crossed, and stared at the notebook for a long minute. "Okay," she said slowly. "Okay, so it's the flies." Rosalie slid the gauze jar toward her and said, "Your turn to make a guess we can test."

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: On a standard 400-metre outdoor track, the 800 metres is exactly two laps, so runners plan the race as a first lap and a second lap.
story:
George had been running himself empty for three weeks, and every time he crossed the line in the eight hundred metres he finished last while his lungs burned. The problem was invisible. Nobody was pushing him, nothing was broken, yet halfway through the race his legs turned to sand. He stood at the edge of the track after practice and watched the older runners, and he noticed something: the ones who won did not look fast at the start. They looked almost lazy.

Henrik jogged over with two water bottles and handed him one. "You went out like a rocket again," Henrik said. "You were leading after the first lap. Then you died."

George frowned. "The first lap. That's four hundred metres, right?" He counted the lanes in his head. The outdoor track looped back to the same white line every four hundred metres, so the whole race was exactly two laps. Two laps meant the race really had two halves, and he had been spending his whole budget on the first one. "It's not a sprint," he said slowly. "It's a first lap and a second lap. I have to save something for the second one."

To test it, he asked Ms. Perera if he could run a time trial before class the next morning. She agreed, holding the stopwatch with her coffee in the other hand. George ran the first lap deliberately behind Henrik, and it felt wrong, like walking past an unopened birthday present. His tendon above his heel twinged at the bend, so he shortened his stride and kept the pace steady. On the second lap he still had legs left. He passed Henrik at the final curve, and the clock showed a time four seconds faster than his best.

At lunch, Arjan spread out the sign-up sheet for Saturday's meet and tapped the eight hundred. "You're doing it," he said, and Henrik nodded so hard it was unanimous before George even opened his mouth.

On Saturday, the starter raised the gun. George reminded himself one more time: two laps, save the second. The gun cracked and the field surged ahead of him, and he held back while every nerve in his body screamed that they were getting away. At the bell, the runner beside him surged wildly toward the far straight, arms pumping like a finish. George blinked. That was one lap too early. The runner looked around, realised his mistake, and groaned out loud. George stayed even, waiting, holding the last of his strength in his legs like a coin in a closed fist. The final curve came up ahead, and George leaned into it.

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons; these versions are called isotopes, but they always have the same number of protons.
story:
The gym smelled like vinegar and baking soda, because somebody's volcano was going off two tables down. Xavier straightened his periodic table poster for the tenth time and checked his stack of element cards again. Carbon, number 6. Oxygen, number 8. All night he had drilled the rule until it felt solid: the big number on each square, the atomic number, told you the protons. He wanted the blue ribbon more than he wanted lunch, and lunch was pizza day.

Dereck leaned over from the next table, where his own poster showed water evaporating from an estuary in careful blue marker arrows. "Judge at three o'clock," he whispered. "She's stopping at everybody."

The judge stopped at the volcano first, then at Dereck, nodding along while he gave a vigorous defense of his arrows. Then she reached Xavier's table, picked up the carbon card, and turned it over slowly. "Tell me about carbon-14," she said. "Is that still carbon?"

Xavier's mind went white. His cards only had plain numbers. Fourteen was not six. If the protons changed, it would be a different element, wouldn't it? But nobody would call something carbon if it wasn't carbon. He stared at the card so long that the judge's pen clicked once, then twice.

A folded square of paper landed on his table. Jemma's handwriting was on the outside fold, and she was watching from the water-quality display with her thumbs up. Xavier's hand drifted toward it, then stopped. Ms. Nasser had said the rules twice this morning: help from a classmate during judging means disqualification. He pushed the note to the corner of the table and turned back to the judge. "It has to still be carbon," he said slowly, testing each step as he said it. "The atomic number, six, that's the protons. That's what makes it carbon. So if carbon-14 is called carbon, the protons are still six. Something else changed." He glanced at the card. "Maybe neutrons. Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons." The judge raised an eyebrow, so he kept going. "Those versions are called isotopes. Same protons, always the same protons, different neutrons."

The judge wrote something on her clipboard and moved on without a word. Xavier waited until she was across the gym, then unfolded Jemma's note with shaking fingers.

"You looked like you were going to evaporate," it read. "P.S. I taped the answer under your carbon card yesterday. You never flipped it over."

Xavier turned the card. There it was in Jemma's handwriting, small and neat: "Same protons. Different neutrons. Isotopes."

"I didn't even need you," he called across the gym, and Jemma just grinned and pointed at the judge, who was writing his table number on something blue.

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: The forearm has two bones: the radius, on the thumb side, and the ulna, on the little-finger side.
story:
Savannah came back to school on Tuesday with a bright green cast from her wrist to her elbow, and by first recess half the playground had gathered around the bench where she sat.

"Which bone did you break?" Cedric asked. "There's more than one in there, you know."

"There's two," Lauralie said. "I saw my cousin's X-ray."

Savannah looked down at her cast. At the hospital, the doctor had held up the film and pointed, but she had been too busy staring at the white line on the black picture to listen. "I don't remember what he said it was called," she admitted. "I just know it was the skinny bit near the middle."

"That's radical," Cedric said, tapping the green plaster with one finger. "But which one is it? They have names, don't they?"

Savannah thought about the X-ray again. She remembered two long pale stripes running side by side, one next to her thumb and one next to her little finger. The doctor's finger had tapped the one on the thumb side. She wiggled her thumb inside the cast, and the muscle pulled tight along the exact place where the ache lived. When she stretched her little finger instead, the pull came from somewhere lower, somewhere that felt fine.

"I think I broke the one on the thumb side," she said slowly. "On the X-ray, the broken one ran along where my thumb is. The other one, the little-finger one, is the one that still feels solid."

"The radius," said Ms. Whitehead, who had crossed the yard on duty and caught the last words. "The thumb-side bone."

"That's it," Savannah said. "He said radius. And the other one is the ulna." She pointed down the cast toward her little finger. "Ulna, that side."

"Prove it," Cedric said.

So Savannah stood up, walked to the water fountain, and turned the handle the way Ms. Whitehead told her to, palm down. Nothing. Then she flipped her arm over, palm up, and pressed the handle with the little-finger side of her cast, and a hot wire of pain shot up toward her elbow. She winced and let go, and the fountain dribbled to a stop.

"That's the ulna side," she said, half laughing, half grimacing. "Definitely the ulna side that still works."

Lauralie wrote "radius, thumb side" on the cast in blue marker, right over the spot where the ache lived, and drew a small crack beside it like a badge.

activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
knowledge_domain: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
fact: Each whole step on the pH scale is a tenfold change, so a solution at pH 3 is ten times more acidic than one at pH 4.
story:
Colton lined up five glasses on the kitchen counter like a tiny laboratory: water, vinegar, baking soda mixed in water, lemon juice, and the dregs of his dad's sports drink. His kit from the science shop had arrived two days ago, a pack of litmus paper strips and a color chart, and he had been waiting all week for a Saturday with nothing else in it. Mustafa had come over, mostly to eat the leftover pizza, but he drifted toward the counter when Colton started tearing strips apart.

"Watch this," Colton said. He dipped a strip into the vinegar and held it up. The paper turned pink-red. "Acid. Blue litmus turns red in acid, and red litmus stays red." He dipped a fresh strip into the baking soda glass, and it stayed blue. "And that one's a base. Red litmus turns blue in a base." He felt like a detective who could interrogate suspects that never said a word out loud.

Mustafa squinted at the chart on the box. "So vinegar's a three and lemon juice is a two." He picked up the lemon juice glass. "Big deal. Three, two, they're neighbors. Two's only a little more acidic than three."

"No, wait." Colton grabbed the chart and read the fine print twice. "It says each whole step is a tenfold change. So pH 3 is ten times more acidic than pH 4." He looked up. "Ten times. Not a little."

Mustafa shook his head. "It's one number apart. One."

Colton took the sports drink glass, which had tested at a 4, and the vinegar at a 3. He couldn't show ten times anything with the strips, since they only gave the number, not the strength. He thought about it while pacing between the counter and the fridge. "You know how you can't see a hormone working, but a tiny amount of it changes a whole lot? This is like that. The scale hides the size of the change." He held up the chart. "pH 3 isn't just one step from pH 4. It's ten times more acidic, right here in the rules."

Mustafa took the lemon juice and vinegar glasses and sniffed each, then set them down slowly. "So lemon juice is ten times more acidic than vinegar." He rubbed the back of his neck. "I told my little sister coke was 'basically water with flavor' yesterday. I'm never going to hear the end of this."

By afternoon they had conquered the whole chart, testing dish soap, rainwater from the windowsill, even a drop of hot sauce Mustafa swore was practically venomous. Every glass sat on the counter with a labeled strip beside it. Then Colton's dad came home, glanced at the row of experiments, and pointed at the sports drink glass. "That was mine, wasn't it."

Colton looked at the pink strip lying next to it. "It was a four."

His dad sighed, picked up the glass, and drained it anyway. "Ten times more acidic than the soap water, and I drank it," he said. "Show me the hot sauce one."

Colton handed him the strip and the chart.

activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
knowledge_domain: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
fact: When cooking several dishes for one meal, start with the one that takes longest and plan backward from the time you want to eat.
story:
Scarlett stood at the steel counter in the back of Mr. Mercer's restaurant, three recipes spread out in front of her. Mr. Mercer had said she could use the kitchen on Sunday nights, when the place was closed, as long as she cleaned everything. Hector and Pierre-Olivier were coming at seven o'clock for the dinner she had promised them: curry, flatbread, and rice.

She read the times first. The curry needed forty minutes. The rice would take twenty. The flatbread was fastest, ten minutes to mix and cook in the hot pan. At first she planned to make them in that order, because that was the order on her list. Then she counted backward on her fingers. If she started the curry at six twenty, it would finish at seven. But if she started everything at six twenty, the flatbread would be cold and stiff by the time they sat down.

She pulled a marker from her pocket and wrote a schedule on a paper towel. They would eat at seven, so the flatbread, the fastest thing, should go in the pan last, at about six fifty. The rice should start at six forty, and the curry, the one that took longest, should be first, at six twenty. She copied the times onto the edge of each recipe so she could not lose them.

While the curry simmered, she checked the little cups of mung beans she had left on the windowsill. Two of them had begun to germinate, tiny white roots poking out of the seeds. She had brought them to show Hector, who insisted you could not grow anything in a restaurant kitchen, and she planned to set the cups on the table as proof.

The rice went on at six forty, and she measured the water twice, because Mr. Mercer had said rice fails on water. At six fifty she mixed the flatbread dough, which she had not planned for. Mixing and rolling took longer than cooking it did, and while she worked, she listened for the rice pot. When the lid rattled, she turned the heat down.

Hector and Pierre-Olivier arrived at seven, right on time. Pierre-Olivier brought a bottle of mango juice and put it in the middle of the table like it was a centerpiece. They argued about whether raisins belonged in curry, which Hector called a controversial opinion and Pierre-Olivier called obvious.

At two minutes past seven, everything came to the table together. The flatbread was warm, the rice steamed, and the curry had thickened exactly as the recipe picture showed. Scarlett watched her friends load their plates and reached for a flatbread while it was still soft.

"Start with the one that takes longest," she said, mostly to herself. Hector looked up, and she pointed at the paper towel schedule hanging over the counter, pinned under the salt shaker. "That's the whole trick."

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: Babies under one year should be put to sleep on their backs, on a firm, flat surface with no pillows, blankets or toys, which lowers the risk of sudden infant death.
story:
Georgia stood in the Hendersons' backyard at 7:58 p.m. holding a squalling baby, and the note in her pocket said the parents would be home at ten. Ten was the deadline. Baby Milo had to be asleep before then, or the Hendersons would come home to a red-faced hurricane and never hire her again.

The note, which Mrs. Henderson had taped to the fridge, read: "Milo's bottle is warm. Safe sleep: back to sleep, firm flat mattress, no pillows, no blankets, no toys. Monitor is on the kitchen counter. Our number is on the back." Georgia read it three times while Milo yanked her earring. Eight months old, and already a meticulous planner of his own escapes.

She got him inside, fed him, burped him twice, and carried him to the crib in the nursery. On the chair beside it sat a fluffy yellow blanket with a duck on it, soft as a cloud, and Georgia reached for it automatically. Her hand stopped in midair. The note. No pillows, no blankets, no toys. She looked at the duck blanket, then at the empty crib, then at the duck blanket again, as if the duck might argue its case. "Sorry, buddy," she told Milo. "You get a bare crib and a firm, flat mattress. That's the whole deal." Milo blinked at her like she had personally cancelled fun.

He screamed anyway. Georgia paced the backyard with him in the dark, whispering every song she half knew, and Jaya texted her from next door: "Is the baby alive? I can hear him from my window. That's impressive." Georgia texted back one-handed: "Barely. I'm not." Jaya replied, "Want backup? I'll monitor him on the monitor while you two stare at the stars. It's very relaxing out here." Georgia, rocking Milo by the rusting swing set, noticed the metal frame was cool and smooth, some silver alloy that never seemed to warm up even in summer, and Milo, cheek against her shoulder, was going heavy and slow.

She laid him down on his back, center of the mattress, tucked nothing around him, and tiptoed out. Through the monitor came one small snort, then quiet breathing, like a tiny accordion. Georgia and Jaya sat on the porch steps with the monitor between them, and at 9:52 the Hendersons' car slid into the driveway. Mrs. Henderson tiptoed in, peeked, and came back whispering, "Asleep on his back, nothing in the crib. You read the note." Georgia nodded solemnly. Jaya raised her hand and said, "I monitored."

activity: to write a paragraph in a new language about plans for next year using the future tense
knowledge_domain: to write a paragraph in a new language about plans for next year using the future tense
fact: Spanish speakers often talk about plans with "ir a" plus an infinitive, as in "Voy a estudiar," meaning "I am going to study."
story:
Naomi sat at Tiago's kitchen table with her Spanish textbook open to the chapter on plans for next year. The textbook only taught one future form, the kind with endings bolted onto the verb, and her paragraph was due Monday. She had written three sentences and erased two of them.

"Stop staring at it," Tiago said, sliding a glass of juice across the table. "It's not an adversary. It's a paragraph."

"Easy for you to say." She was hesitant to admit it, but she wanted to tell someone, so she did. "I got a C on the last one because I guessed at the forms. I'm not guessing this time."

Tiago's grandmother came in from the garden with a basket of tomatoes and asked, in Spanish, what they were doing. Naomi tried her question out: next year, what would she do? The grandmother answered without pausing. "Voy a estudiar," she said, and then more words Naomi didn't catch, something about a garden and a trip.

Naomi wrote the phrase down fast. She had seen "ir" before, the verb that meant to go, and she knew an infinitive when she saw one. Her textbook chapter never mentioned putting them together like that. She looked at her notes, then at the grandmother, who was still sorting tomatoes. Could Spanish speakers really talk about plans with "ir a" plus an infinitive? It sounded like English, saying you were going to do something, but she had been wrong before when things sounded like English.

She tested it. "Voy a jugar?" she asked, holding up her draft, and pointed at a line about playing on the soccer team next fall. The grandmother nodded and corrected nothing. Naomi tried a third one, "Voy a viajar," and got another nod, plus a smile that suggested she was saying it well enough for a person who talked to tomatoes.

By the time the paragraph was finished, five of her six sentences used the new pattern, and each one had survived the grandmother. Naomi copied the final version into her notebook while Tiago teased her about taking over his kitchen.

Monday, Mr. Gagnon handed back the paragraphs at the end of class. Naomi's came back with a red circle around her first sentence and a single note: "We don't cover this until spring. Where did you learn it?"

She thought of the basket of tomatoes and almost laughed. "Next year," she said, "I'm going to ask your questions earlier."

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: Teasing often depends on an audience, so walking away with the targeted classmate, saying something like "Come on, let's go," can end it without a confrontation.
story:
The kitchen at Lyam's house smelled like popcorn and someone's spilled root beer, and James was stacking cups by the sink when he heard the laughter change pitch across the room. A boy from his science class had Jayla's phone in his hand, holding it above her head, reading her game notifications out loud in a squeaky voice. "Ooh, level forty in Cat Garden, everybody." A ring of kids had formed around them, and every time Jayla jumped for the phone, the circle laughed again.

James felt his face go hot. He had promised himself after the incident in the cafeteria last month, when his sharp comeback had only made things louder, that he would handle the next moment differently, though he had not figured out how. He watched the boy's eyes flick toward the audience after every joke, checking for laughs the way a performer checks a crowd. That was the pattern. The teasing was not really about Jayla's phone at all. It was about the circle of faces, feeding it. Take away the audience, James thought, and there might be nothing left to perform for.

He crossed the room anyway, skeptical of his own theory, and tried a joke first. "Give it back, man, your solo act is bombing." The circle laughed, but at him now, and the boy grinned wider because a second performer had joined the show. James felt the old resentment rising, the urge to make the boy resent him back, and he recognized it as a trap. More words meant more show. So he stopped talking to the boy entirely, turned to Jayla, and said, "Come on, let's go. Lyam needs help with the snacks in the basement."

Jayla blinked at him, then dropped her arms. "Fine," she said, and followed him toward the basement door. Behind them the boy said something about level forty again, but his voice had gone flat, and when James glanced back, the circle was already drifting apart toward the music. Nobody laughed at a joke with no one watching it land.

In the basement, among the bags of chips, Jayla folded her arms and gave her verdict. "That was the third time he's done that this year, and the first time anyone left with me instead of arguing for me." She pulled the chip bag open. "Also, there is no snack emergency down here, is there?"

"No," James admitted. "I made that up."

The basement door creaked open above them, and the boy came down two steps, holding out Jayla's phone. "You left this on the counter," he mumbled, not quite meeting anyone's eyes. He set it on the bottom stair and went back up.

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: At 5 percent interest compounded once a year, $1,000 grows to $1,276.28 after five years.
story:
Max had the folded paper in his pocket all afternoon, the one his grandfather had written on at Thanksgiving: "You save $1,000, I'll add $50 every year for five years." At the food court table, between a tray of fries and Cynthia's untouched smoothie, he finally spread it out next to the bank flyer he'd picked up at the kiosk by the escalator.

"The bank says five percent," Cynthia said, leaning over it. "That's fifty dollars a year too. Same thing."

"Maybe." Max turned the flyer over. In small print it said interest compounded once a year, and next to that, a little table showed what a $1,000 account would be worth later on. The last row of the table said $1,276.28.

Milania dropped into the seat across from them and stole a fry. "What are we doing, a budget meeting?" She said it lightly, but Max noticed she kept looking at the paper, and her sneaker was tapping the floor, quick and steady. Something was on her mind besides the fries.

"Grandpa's deal ends at $1,250," Max said. "Fifty a year, five years. But the bank's table says $1,276.28. That's twenty-six dollars and twenty-eight cents more, and it's the same rate." He tapped the number twice.

"Then the table's wrong," Cynthia said. "Or there's a trick. Banks love tricks."

Max wanted to know which it was. He took out his phone and opened the calculator, and Milania stopped tapping her sneaker. "Can I ask something?" she said. "Is this about the guitar?" Max kept his eyes on the screen. "It's about math," he said, which was true, and also not.

He tested it the only way he could think of. If the bank added fifty dollars and then treated that fifty like part of the money that earned interest the next year, the total would grow by a little more each time, and the growth itself would grow. That was the variable he couldn't see on the flyer, the thing hiding underneath the flat five percent. He worked through year one, year two, year three, his thumb moving slower each time as the decimals got longer. Cynthia watched over his shoulder without breathing on his neck, which for Cynthia was a serious effort.

At year five his screen said 1276.28. He checked it twice. The table wasn't wrong, and the bank wasn't cheating anybody; the money was just doing something he hadn't known money could do. Simple interest stayed simple, and the other kind, the kind that fed on itself, ended twenty-six dollars and twenty-eight cents higher. He looked up to tell them, and Milania was already standing, pulling her jacket on.

"I have to tell you before I lose my nerve," she said. "I've been saving for the same guitar. Since September. That's why I asked." The food court noise went on around them, trays and footsteps and a toddler shrieking near the pretzel stand, but at their table it went quiet.

Max folded the bank flyer and put it in his pocket, next to his grandfather's note. "Then you're going to want to see this table," he said, and slid the calculator across the table to her.

"You'd really show me the numbers? Even though we want the same one?"

"It's not a competition if we both know the math," Max said. "Venomous loses to twenty-six dollars and twenty-eight cents every time."

Milania laughed, sat back down, and pulled the flyer toward her with both hands.
